title: The Copper Plate That Checked the Arab Advance

title_i18n.en: The Copper Plate That Checked the Arab Advance

subtitle: How frontier kings and a copper plate marked the edge of an empire
era: Arab frontier raids and Gurjara-Pratihara rise, c. 724-743 CE
region: Rajasthan, Malwa and Navsari in Gujarat
moral: History often turns when many local defenders hold their ground.

sources.citation: Navsari copper plate of Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin, 745 CE, edited in Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. III
sources.note: Near-contemporary Chalukya-feudatory record of defeating a mleccha army in Gujarat.

sources.citation: Gwalior prashasti of Mihira Bhoja, c. 860 CE, edited in CII Vol. III
sources.note: Later Pratihara panegyric crediting Nagabhata I with repulsing the invincible mlechha army.

sources.citation: Ahmad al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, 9th century CE; Andre Wink, Al-Hind, Vol. I, 1990
sources.note: Arab-side campaign notices and modern synthesis of why expansion stalled.

panels.shot: dramatic split-composition, one half showing Nagabhata I on a rampart, the other Avanijanashraya before a scribe etching a plate

dialogue.text: A copper plate in Navsari, a praise-song in Gwalior, and Arab chronicles in Baghdad together trace how Nagabhata and Avanijanashraya held the eastern edge of the Caliph’s advance.

panels.shot: wide aerial over the Indus and Sindh, with faint arrows pushing eastward

dialogue.text: After Sindh fell to the armies of the Umayyad caliphs, their governors looked east. Beyond the Indus lay Malwa, Rajasthan, and the rich ports of Gujarat.

panels.shot: interior, dim Abbasid court archival hall with a scholar reading

dialogue.text: Centuries later, Ahmad al-Baladhuri would write in Baghdad of raids launched from Sindh, naming towns and rivers, but not of any lasting conquest beyond that frontier.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nagabhata I in a frontier fort, map before him

dialogue.text: On this frontier, new powers stirred. One was Nagabhata, first of the Gurjara-Pratiharas, holding lines in Rajasthan and Malwa as Arab probes searched for weak seams.

panels.shot: wide shot of Avanijanashraya in a Gujarat coastal town, ships behind

dialogue.text: Farther south-west in Gujarat, Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin served as a Chalukya feudatory. His task: guard the coastal routes, where Arab fleets and columns could converge.

panels.shot: low wide shot of an Arab column crossing a semi-arid plain

dialogue.text: Baladhuri’s pages recall Arab commanders pushing toward the lands of the ‘Rur’ and beyond, leading contingents from Sindh into the plains east and south of the desert.

panels.shot: close-up on Nagabhata I’s face, lit by firelight, thoughtful

dialogue.text: We do not have Nagabhata’s own words. What we have are later praises carved in stone, remembering how he faced what one inscription would call an ‘invincible mleccha army’.

panels.shot: close-up of hands carving letters into stone at Gwalior

dialogue.text: In Gwalior, much later, Mihira Bhoja’s panegyrist would recall Nagabhata as the one who repulsed that army. Epigraphers call it the Gwalior prashasti, and treat it as dynastic memory.

panels.shot: dynamic mid-shot of Nagabhata I riding out of a fort gate with cavalry

dialogue.text: The inscription gives no date, no named battlefield, only boast and outcome. But between those lines, historians see a series of clashes that hardened a frontier across Rajasthan and Malwa.

panels.shot: long shot of Navsari countryside, Arab and Indian forces facing each other

dialogue.text: In Gujarat, one engagement came into sharper focus. There, near Navsari, an army from Sindh advanced. Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin met them, and this time, his scribes recorded the victory in copper.

panels.shot: medium shot of Avanijanashraya commanding, arm raised, elephants ahead

dialogue.speaker: nagabhata_i_and_avanijanashraya_pulakeshin
dialogue.text: Steady the line. Let them feel the weight of this land.

panels.shot: medium shot of Avanijanashraya commanding, arm raised, elephants ahead

dialogue.speaker: nagabhata_i_and_avanijanashraya_pulakeshin
dialogue.text: Steady the line. Let them feel the weight of this land.

panels.shot: close-up on the Navsari copper plate being held up to the light

dialogue.text: Dated around 745 CE, the Navsari plate names him Avanijanashraya, protector of earth, and declares that he defeated a mleccha army. Unlike legend, this document stands almost beside the event.

panels.shot: interior of a Chalukya court, ministers listening to reading of the plate

dialogue.text: The plate credits him as a loyal feudatory of his Chalukya overlord. Its purpose was land grant and royal favour, yet in its flourish it preserves a frontier clash with extraordinary clarity.

panels.shot: map shot, slow zoom on a line arching from Sindh, bending, then stopping

dialogue.text: Modern histories, reading Arabic texts alongside these plates, see not one single ‘Battle of Rajasthan’, but a frontier series. Raids pressed in, met fort by fort, and then their momentum ebbed.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nagabhata and Avanijanashraya shown separately, both in thoughtful repose

dialogue.text: For the caliphal governors in Sindh, these setbacks, distance, and other priorities made deep conquest eastward unattractive. For Nagabhata and Avanijanashraya, they were chances to consolidate.

panels.shot: wide view of a Pratihara court, anachronistic hint of later power

dialogue.text: Out of Nagabhata’s era grew the Gurjara-Pratihara kingdom, one of north India’s great powers. Its poets anchored their claim not only in lineage, but in that remembered stand against the mlecchas.

panels.shot: close-up of a bard reciting before Rajput listeners, with shadowy imagery of Bappa Rawal behind

dialogue.text: Much later, songs in Rajasthan would place names like Bappa Rawal into these struggles, weaving legend onto history. Inscriptions, however, keep their silence on him for this frontier.

panels.shot: modern historian at a desk with books, copper plate facsimile, and Arabic text

dialogue.text: Today, scholars lay these fragments together: Arabic narratives, copper grants, stone eulogies. Where they agree, we glimpse the frontier; where they differ, we see how memory shapes power.

panels.shot: final wide shot over the Rajasthan-Gujarat landscape at sunrise, ghostly outlines of forts and routes

dialogue.text: The Arab advance east of the Indus slowed not at a single miracle battle, but along a line of local defenders like Nagabhata and Avanijanashraya, whose quiet victories still mark where empires stopped.
